title: Insurance claims automation: can AI speed claims and stay compliant?
description: Insurance claims automation for P&C carriers, MGAs and TPAs: what AI takes on, what adjusters keep, state AI rules and claim deadlines.
verdict: AI takes the first pass: intake, documents, triage, fraud flags, reserve suggestions. Adjusters keep coverage, payment and the customer.[^1][^2]
Regulators apply the same unfair-claims rules to AI-assisted decisions. Texas expects a person to agree before acting.[^3][^4]
Nearly half of US P&C premium sits where the NAIC AI bulletin applies, by our count.[^5][^6]
No claims AI vendor we checked publishes a price. Start with intake on one line, tested on your closed claims.[^7][^8]
This page covers property and casualty (P&C) claims. Health claims follow different laws on medical necessity and AI.[^9][^10]

headings.what-it-is: What is insurance claims automation, and what does it change?
headings.human-role: Who on your claims team keeps the decision?
headings.team-after: What does your claims team do once AI takes the first pass?

summary: Insurance claims automation, or AI claims processing, gives software the first pass on a claim: reading the report, documents and photos, then flagging it.[^11][^12] Adjusters still decide coverage, reserves and payment.[^1] It works only if the file shows who decided what, inside each state's deadlines.[^4][^13]

answers.human-role: The adjuster keeps the decision on coverage, the reserve, any denial and the customer, and supervisors approve payments within their authority.[^1][^3]
answers.team-after: Adjusters spend the freed time on investigation, coverage analysis and customers, while intake reps confirm AI-filled fields instead of keying them.[^17][^18]
answers.example: On one water-damage claim, AI fills the fields, quotes the policy clauses and drafts the acknowledgment letter, and the adjuster decides coverage, reserve and payment.[^4]
answers.recipes: Small teams start with AI at intake and documents, multi-client TPAs add triage and deadline tracking, and document-heavy lines use summaries with citations.[^8][^11][^34]
answers.rules: The NAIC AI bulletin, each state's unfair-claims law and deadlines, and state guidance such as Texas Bulletin B-0003-26 apply to AI claims decisions.[^11][^3][^4] Health claims follow separate rules.[^10]
answers.benchmark: Run the tool in shadow mode on 200 to 500 of your closed claims, then compare its fields, flags and reserves with what your adjusters recorded.[^54]
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI claims processing goes wrong through biased fraud scores, one bad rule repeated on every claim, missed state deadlines, and adjusters stuck fixing its mistakes.[^15][^3][^54][^21]
answers.something-else: Pick something else when your claims are mostly simple auto damage, your real problem is talking to claimants, or your core claims system is the bottleneck.[^7][^24]

humanRole: Adjuster: decides coverage, sets the reserve, signs any denial and talks to the customer.[^1][^3] Texas expects a person to review and agree with any consequential AI decision before action.[^4]
Claims supervisor or examiner: approves payments within their authority and spot-checks AI-filled files.[^1] The insurer answers for every AI-supported decision, vendor tools included.[^11][^14]

Special investigations unit (SIU) investigator: works each fraud flag as a lead to investigate, not a finding.[^3] A homeowners' lawsuit alleges an insurer's claim-screening algorithms scrutinised Black policyholders more; that claim survived dismissal.[^15][^16]
Head of claims with the compliance lead: own the written AI program and the list of AI tools in use.[^11][^14] Both report to senior management, which answers to the board.[^11]
teamAfter: Adjusters spend freed time on investigation, coverage analysis and customers, a TPA's own survey reports.[^17] Analysts see the next value in the roughly 15% of claims that are complex.[^12]
Intake reps confirm AI-filled fields instead of keying them. One TPA says intake fell from 10 days to 36 hours (vendor claim).[^18]
Customers still get a person on hard claims: 77% prefer a human for complex or emotional claims (vendor survey).[^19]
Among US firms using AI, 66% use it only to help existing staff, and 2% report AI-related job cuts.[^20] In one labor study, 49% of carriers expect to add staff.[^21]

example.input: Illustrative: a homeowners water-damage claim at a regional carrier, or a TPA handling it for an MGA. The file holds the first report of loss, 14 photos, the policy declarations and endorsements, a plumber's invoice and a mitigation estimate.
example.output: AI fills the claim fields, flags the ones it is unsure of, quotes the water and mold clauses with page numbers, and tags it desk-adjustable. It drafts the acknowledgment letter and sets a deadline task: 7 days in Florida, 15 in Texas.[^22][^23] The adjuster confirms coverage, sets the reserve, calls the customer and approves payment; the tool never sends a denial.[^4]

recipes.name: 1. Small claims team (MGA or small carrier): AI at intake and documents
recipes.when: Teams on an existing claims system who want fewer re-keyed fields and on-time acknowledgments. A review site lists Snapsheet, Hi Marley and Ushur as fits under 5,000 claims a month.[^8]
flow: Intake rep: confirm the fields AI filled from the first report
Desk adjuster: check the AI coverage summary against the policy, then set the reserve
Desk adjuster: send the acknowledgment letter AI drafted, inside the state deadline
Claims supervisor: spot-check 10% of AI-filled files each week
Compliance lead: add the tool to the AI inventory the bulletin asks for
recipes.cost: Not published; vendors quote by claim volume or users, so ask for a price on your volume.[^24][^8] Size it against your adjusting cost, about 9 cents per premium dollar across US P&C.[^6][^30]

recipes.name: 2. Multi-client TPA or mid-size carrier: triage plus deadline tracking
recipes.when: TPAs handling claims for several carriers or self-insured clients across states, each with its own service levels. Carriers will ask about your AI, since the bulletin makes them answer for outside tools.[^11]
flow: Claims ops lead: have the tool score each new claim for complexity and litigation risk
Claims ops lead: have the tool open a state-deadline task on every new claim
Claims supervisor: assign claims by score
Adjuster: decide coverage and set the reserve
SIU investigator: work the ranked fraud referrals and record which proved out
Client service lead: report deadline compliance per client each month
recipes.cost: Not published; triage tools are licensed by claim volume or line.[^8] Late-reported claims carry about ten times the litigation risk (TPA survey), which is where triage pays.[^17]

recipes.name: 3. Document-heavy lines (workers' comp, casualty, bodily injury): summaries with citations
recipes.when: Teams buried in medical records, legal demands and invoices. In a survey of 263 insurance executives, claim summaries saved 35-45% of time on complex claims.[^34]
flow: Claims ops lead: route medical records, demands and invoices to the reading tool
Adjuster or nurse case manager: check each fact against the page the summary cites
Claims supervisor: approve any reserve change
Adjuster: send the checked summary to defense counsel
recipes.cost: Not published; document tools price by volume and lines.[^8] Budget review time too: a Nordic insurer's tool read 70% of documents correctly.[^32]

ownData.title: The 10 biggest P&C states: AI bulletin status and claim deadlines
ownData.intro: We ranked states by 2025 P&C direct premium (NAIC), then read each AI rule status on the NAIC map of 13 Nov 2026.[^6][^5] Six of the ten adopted the NAIC AI bulletin, two run their own rules and two have neither.[^5] Texas alone lifted the adopted share of US premium from 37.1% to 46.6%.[^5][^36]
rows: Accept or deny within 40 days of proof; pay within 30 days of accepting[^38]
Adopted: B-0003-26, Jun 2026; expects human review[^4][^5]
15 business days after all items (45 more with notice); pay within 5 business days[^23]
Not adopted; AI-denial bills died Mar 2026[^5][^39]
Pay or deny residential property claims within 60 days of notice[^22]
Own rules: DFS Circular Letter 7, Jul 2024[^5][^40]
Accept or deny within 15 business days of proof of loss[^42]
Pay within 30 days of affirming liability; written delay notice by day 75[^43]
Motor vehicle: 15 days after proof of loss. Fire: 60 days, then pay within 10[^44]
Accept or deny within 15 working days of proofs of loss[^45]
Pay first-party claims within 30 calendar days of proof of loss[^46]
30 days to say what proof of loss is needed[^47]
Timely if paid within 60 days of proof of loss; after that, 12% interest[^47]
No fixed day count; must affirm or deny within a reasonable time after proof of loss[^48]
Adopted: 46.6%; own rules (CA, CO, NY): 20.8%; neither: about 32%[^5][^6]
15 business or working days (TX, NY, PA) to 60 days (FL, MI)
ownData.note: Zavient check, 26 Nov 2026, from the NAIC state premium table (Arizona split from Arkansas by hand) and each state's rule text.[^6] The NAIC map dated 13 Nov 2026 counts 30 jurisdictions; trackers reading other versions count 29.[^5][^49][^36] Deadlines show the main first-party rule only; Georgia mixes motor and fire rules, and none of this is legal advice.

rules.name: NAIC Model Bulletin: Use of AI Systems by Insurers
rules.what: It names claim administration, payment and fraud detection as covered uses.[^11] Decisions must not be inaccurate, arbitrary, capricious or unfairly discriminatory.[^11][^50] You answer for vendor AI, so keep it in your written AI program.[^11]

rules.name: NAIC Unfair Claims Settlement Practices Act (Model 900)
rules.status: Model law; states adopted their own versions (NAIC chart MC-50)
rules.what: It bars refusing to pay without a reasonable investigation, and failing to explain a denial.[^3][^51] A rule built into software runs on every claim, so one bad rule can become a general business practice.[^3][^52]

rules.name: NAIC Unfair P&C Claims Settlement Practices Model Regulation (Model 902)
rules.what: The model clock: acknowledge in 15 days, accept or deny within 21 days of proof of loss, pay within 30.[^13] Your state's own rule governs; see our table above.[^51]

rules.name: Texas Commissioner's Bulletin B-0003-26
rules.what: TDI expects a person to review and agree with every consequential AI decision before action.[^4] It ties AI use to the Chapter 542 prompt-payment deadlines.[^4][^23]

rules.name: Florida HB 527 and SB 202 (2026)
rules.what: They would have required a qualified human professional to review AI output and be named on any claim denial.[^39][^53] HB 527 passed the House 108-0 before it died, so the idea may return.[^39]

rules.name: California fair claims rules (10 CCR 2695) and Bulletin 2022-5
rules.what: California issues its own AI guidance instead of the NAIC bulletin.[^5] Its 2026 exam of one insurer's wildfire claims found 398 violations in 114 of 220 sampled files, many on missed deadlines.[^54]

rules.name: NAIC AI Risk Evaluation Supplement
rules.status: Piloted by 12 states Mar-Sep 2026; version 7.0 up for adoption Nov 2026
rules.what: Examiners will use it to ask which AI you use, how you govern it and which systems are high-risk.[^55][^56] P&C insurers made up 55% of the pilot survey responses.[^56]

rules.name: Health claims: Medicare Advantage rule and state laws
rules.what: Medicare Advantage decisions must rest on the patient's own circumstances, though an algorithm may assist.[^10][^57] California bars AI as the sole basis for medical-necessity denials.[^58][^9] None of this binds P&C claims.[^59]

howToTest: Pick one line or office and pull 200 to 500 of its closed claims from the last 12 months, split by state and outcome. Examiners sample closed files the same way; California's 2026 exam sampled 220.[^54]
Record today's numbers on those files: days to acknowledge, decide and pay, the share inside each state's deadline, reopens and complaints.[^23][^37]
Run the tool in shadow mode on the same files. It fills fields, scores triage and fraud and suggests reserves, but changes nothing.

Score document reading field by field against what the adjuster recorded, counting wrong fields as well as missing ones. Published rates run from 70% read correctly to 87% handled with no manual touch.[^32][^28]

Compare flags with what happened: how many fraud flags SIU would have opened and proved, and how many simple files went to litigation. Late reporting carries about ten times the litigation risk (TPA survey).[^17]
Compare reserve suggestions with the adjuster's reserve and with what the claim finally cost, at 30 and 90 days.
Check for unfair discrimination: compare flag rates and days to payment across ZIP codes and other proxies for protected groups.[^11][^60]
Price the lift in dollars: hours saved times loaded adjuster cost, plus late-payment interest avoided, such as Michigan's 12%.[^47][^1] Set it against your adjusting cost baseline.[^6]
Write the decision rule before go-live: which outputs a person confirms, who signs off and what the file shows. Texas expects that sign-off, and examiners will ask for the record.[^4][^55]
watchOuts: Biased fraud and routing scores. A homeowners' lawsuit alleges an insurer's tools gave Black policyholders' claims more scrutiny; test flag rates by area before go-live and each quarter.[^15][^60]
One bad rule, repeated on every claim, can become a general business practice under unfair-claims law.[^3][^52] Have compliance review each automated rule before it runs.
Missed state deadlines. California's 2026 wildfire-claims exam cited missed 15-, 40- and 30-day clocks; have the tool open a deadline task on day one.[^54][^37]

Adjusters fixing the AI instead of being helped by it: one adjuster describes 15 to 20 minutes correcting AI mistakes.[^21][^19] Show the source page for every fact the tool pulls, and track rework time.
Vendor black boxes: you answer for vendor AI, and in a health case a court ordered an insurer to show how its tool worked.[^11][^61] Put audit and testing rights in the contract.

A thinner talent pipeline: junior adjuster postings are down about half since early 2024, and 25% of adjusters may retire by 2027 (TPA survey).[^21][^17] Keep juniors on AI-checked files so they still learn.

faq.a: Yes, for the first pass: intake, document reading, triage, fraud flags and reserve suggestions.[^11][^12] In the regulators' 2022 survey, 96 of 193 auto insurers used AI to inform adjusters and none used it to deny claims.[^2]

faq.q: Is AI taking over claims adjuster jobs?
faq.a: Not on the evidence: BLS expects about 21,600 openings a year to 2035, even as total jobs dip 6%.[^1] In one labor study, 49% of carriers expect to add staff and 11% to cut.[^21] Among US firms using AI, 2% report AI-related job cuts.[^20]

faq.q: How do you automate claims processing?
faq.a: Start with first-report intake and document reading on one line of business, test on closed files, then add triage.[^12][^11] Keep coverage and payment decisions with adjusters.[^4]

faq.q: Can an insurer deny a P&C claim using AI alone?
faq.a: No P&C state law bans it outright yet; Florida's attempt died in March 2026.[^39][^59] Denials still need a reasonable investigation and a stated reason, and Texas expects a person to agree first.[^3][^4]

faq.q: Does the AI bulletin reach a TPA or MGA handling claims for a carrier?
faq.a: Indirectly. It is addressed to insurers, but they stay responsible for AI from outside firms, so expect questions in your contracts and audits.[^11][^62]

faq.q: Do the same rules apply to health insurance claims?
faq.a: No. Health claims run on medical-necessity rules, and California bars AI as the sole basis for those denials.[^58][^9] Medicare Advantage decisions must rest on each patient's circumstances.[^10]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when you have no data team, run a common core claims system and the job is standard: first reports, photos, documents.[^63] Purchased AI tools succeed about 67% of the time; internal builds about a third as often.[^64][^65]
buyVsBuild.build: Build, or configure heavily, when your own claims history is the edge or you must show a regulator every rule.[^11] Either way, 45% of insurers name data quality as a barrier, so clean the claim data first.[^34] Only 24% of insurance leaders are very confident they'd pass an AI governance review in 90 days.[^66]

pickElse: Mostly simple auto physical damage: a photo-estimating network such as CCC, Tractable or Snapsheet already does this job.[^7][^26]
The problem is talking to claimants, not reading files: a texting platform such as Hi Marley may fix more.[^24][^7]
Your core claims system is the bottleneck: upgrade or replace it first, such as Guidewire, Duck Creek or Five Sigma.[^7] AI on a system nobody trusts adds rework.
Low volume across varied lines: rules in your current system plus a weekly report on state deadlines may cost less than AI.[^13][^23]

offer.heading: Which part of your claims process should AI take first?
offer.body: Intake on one line usually comes first, tested on your own closed claims. Bring us your claims intake and your list of states, and in 30 minutes we map first report to decision against each state's deadline. You leave with the first step, a closed-file test and a before-and-after measure, with no sales pitch.

reviews.notes: Dana, as COO: could see who decides what and the state deadlines, but the bottom line never said where to start. The no-price bullet now names the first step: intake on one line, tested on closed claims. 'Straight-through' was jargon; it now reads 'handled with no manual touch'. No sourced time-to-pilot figure exists in the research, so none is given.

Dana, as head of claims operations: the five-column state table was heavy on a phone, so the Texas status and deadline cells were cut to the essentials. 'Final incurred losses' became 'what the claim finally cost'. Every recipe step already names the role doing it.

Asked whether one office or one line can pilot first and what it does to margin. The first test step now starts with one line or office. The margin baseline is on the page twice: about 9 cents of each premium dollar goes on adjusting, and each recipe's cost line says to size quotes against it.

Head of claims at a regional carrier, MGA or TPA: the SIU bullet leaned on the bulletin for a point it doesn't make; it now rests on the unfair-claims law's reasonable-investigation duty. The example now shows the tool flagging fields it is unsure of. North Carolina's 30-day acknowledgment was confirmed in G.S. 58-3-100(c). Health is kept to one bullet, one rule and one FAQ.

Steve gets the answer in 10 seconds and sees plainly that no vendor publishes a price; no Zavient price is shown. His data worry was missing, so buy-or-build now cites the 45% of insurers naming data quality as a barrier. Security has no claims-specific source in the research, so it is covered only as contract audit rights. Every mid-size result on the page is a vendor case, labelled as such; no independent case from a firm his size exists.
